title: Stocks after midterm elections: 10 takeaways for investors

 How stocks perform after midterm elections, from BlackRock's midterm-year caution to SentimenTrader's November-to-April pattern, with Democrats holding majorities in both chambers of Congress
 1 / 12 List slides Stocks after midterm elections: what 10 market findings show List slides Previous Start over By Colleen Cabili · Updated November 6, 2026 Add QZ to Google Illustration: Quartz
 The 2026 midterm elections have reshaped the balance of power in Washington. The Associated Press has Democrats holding majorities in both the House and the Senate, with some races still uncalled. President Donald Trump still has half of his term left. For investors, that split raises a familiar question: what happens to stocks after midterm elections?
 Markets did not wait for every race to be called. Investors have already seen near-term price changes in stocks viewed as helped or hurt by policy and by the shift in power. Oil, gold and cryptocurrency have shown similar moves. The S&P 500 ended a three-day losing streak on Tuesday.
 The longer record points in a different direction from those early swings. Many experts believe election outcomes have a limited effect on returns for the market as a whole. Policy changes can still move specific stocks, commodities and cryptocurrencies.
 BlackRock $BLK recently wrote that midterm election years tend not to be the strongest years for stocks. Bespoke Investment Group urged calm. Its analysts noted that stocks have kept rising since the Great Financial Crisis, even as control in Washington moved among different party combinations. "While power in DC has changed hands again and again, there has been one constant: the S&P 500 has risen during every one of the last nine sessions," the firm said.
 Franklin Templeton found that when a Republican is president, the party split in Congress after the midterms appears to matter relatively little for returns. The firm put the average 12-month stock return at around 15% since the 1950s under Republican presidents, whichever party controls each chamber. Its research also found that a setup like today's, with Democrats holding majorities in both houses, has been the most common one in that period.
 SentimenTrader adds a seasonal angle. The firm found that the stock market has not fallen between Nov. 1 of a midterm year and April of the following year at any point since the 1930s. Past patterns do not amount to a forecast. The 10 slides that follow take a selection of these findings one at a time, from the near-term market moves to the longer historical record.
 Democrats win House and Senate majorities in the 2026 midterms 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Democrats hold majorities in both the House and the Senate after the 2026 midterm elections, according to the Associated Press. Some races were still uncalled when Investopedia reported the result.
 The outcome produces a divided government. President Donald Trump, a Republican, has half of his term left. He serves that remaining half alongside a Congress in which Democrats control both chambers.
 The open contests leave one question unsettled. The AP call shows which party holds the House and which holds the Senate. It does not yet show how large either majority will be. Final seat totals depend on the races not yet called.
 A Republican president paired with a Democratic Congress is the setting for the market question that follows the vote. Investopedia's explainer on the result, written by David Marino-Nachison, was first published Nov. 3, 2026, and updated Nov. 4. It looks at how stocks have tended to behave around midterm elections.
 Why election outcomes have a limited effect on overall stock market returns 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Many experts believe election results do relatively little to move returns for the stock market as a whole, according to Investopedia. Policy changes that follow a vote could still move specific stocks, commodities and cryptocurrencies.
 The view rests on a split between the market and the assets inside it. A market-level return measures a broad group of companies together, often through an index such as the S&P 500. A single stock, a commodity or a cryptocurrency is a much narrower holding.
 That split shapes how an election result can be read. A change in party control can put one company, one industry or one asset in the spotlight. A sharp move in that holding does not automatically show up in the index-level return.
 Two firms cited by Investopedia support the broad-market side of the argument. Bespoke Investment Group noted that the S&P 500 has kept rising since the Great Financial Crisis as control in Washington changed hands. Franklin Templeton found that under a Republican president, the party split in Congress after the midterms appears to matter relatively little for returns.
 Neither finding names a winning party. Both describe market-level results that held up across different combinations of power in Washington.
 The view does not say elections are irrelevant to investors. It holds that policy effects are more likely to surface in narrower slices of the market than in the market as a whole.
 Policy-sensitive stocks move after a shift in power in Washington 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Shares seen as winners or losers from a change in Washington's balance of power have already posted near-term price moves after the 2026 midterm elections, Investopedia reports.
 The shift behind those moves is a Congress in which Democrats hold majorities in both chambers, according to the Associated Press. Some races were still uncalled when the report was published.
 The report sorts the affected shares into two groups. The first holds companies the market views as helped by policy or by the change in power. The second holds companies viewed as hurt by those same forces.
 The moves are short-term ones. The report covers price changes in the immediate aftermath of the vote. It does not say whether those changes held.
 The report names no companies or sectors in either group. It gives no figures for how far any of these shares rose or fell. The direction of the moves is reported, but not their size or how widely they spread.
 The report separates these moves from the broader market. Its key takeaways say policy changes could move specific stocks. That point is about individual companies rather than market-level returns.
 Oil, gold and cryptocurrency prices after the midterm results 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Oil, gold and cryptocurrency prices have already shown near-term changes linked to the 2026 midterm results. Investopedia reports that investors saw these moves as the balance of power in Washington shifted.
 The report does not give a direction or a size for any of these moves. It does not say whether oil, gold or cryptocurrency rose or fell, or by how much. It describes the changes only as near-term.
 These assets sit in the part of the market that policy can move directly. Investopedia's key takeaways say specific commodities and cryptocurrencies could be moved by policy changes. The same applies to individual stocks.
 That sets them apart from the broad market. The report frames election outcomes as having a limited effect on market-level returns, while leaving room for individual assets to react.
 The results behind these moves were not final when the report was updated. The Associated Press has Democrats holding majorities in both the House and the Senate, with some races still uncalled.
 BlackRock on why stocks rarely post their best results in midterm years 
 Illustration: Quartz
 BlackRock $BLK recently wrote that stocks tend not to post their strongest results during midterm election years. The remark describes a general tendency across past election cycles.
 As reported, the note gave no figures. It does not say how much weaker midterm years have been. It also does not say how often they have trailed other years, or which index and time span the comparison covers.
 That leaves the point as a direction rather than a measured gap. It indicates that midterm years have not usually been the standout years for stocks. It does not indicate how large any shortfall has been.
 A midterm year is the second year of a U.S. president's four-year term. Voters choose every member of the House and part of the Senate. Control of either chamber can change hands, while the presidency is not on the ballot.
 BlackRock has also pointed out that stock markets often do well once an election lessens uncertainty. That remark concerns the stretch after a vote is settled. The midterm-year comment covers the calendar year as a whole, including the months before any results are known. The two points describe different windows of time rather than opposing views.
 Bespoke Investment Group on S&P 500 gains through shifts in party control 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Bespoke Investment Group urged investors to stay calm after the 2026 midterms. Its analysts noted that the stock market has kept climbing since the Great Financial Crisis, even as control of Washington moved among different party combinations.
 The firm summed up that record in a single line: "While power in DC has changed hands again and again, there has been one constant: the S&P 500 has risen during every one of the last nine sessions."
 The unit of measure in that quote is the session. Bespoke did not frame its finding in calendar years or in individual elections. The claim covers only the nine sessions the firm cites.
 The observation concerns the S&P 500 as a whole. It says nothing about how any single company, sector or asset fared during those stretches.
 The finding also describes direction rather than size. Bespoke's quote says the index rose in each session, but it gives no figure for how much.
 The 2026 vote brings another shift in power. The Associated Press has Democrats holding majorities in both the House and the Senate, with some races still uncalled.
 Bespoke's record shows how the index behaved through earlier changes in control. It does not predict how the S&P 500 will move under the new Congress.
 Franklin Templeton on average 12-month returns under Republican presidents 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Franklin Templeton puts the average 12-month stock return at around 15% since the 1950s when a Republican is president. That average holds whichever party controls each chamber of Congress after the midterms.
 The asset manager's broader point concerns the partisan lineup on Capitol Hill. Franklin Templeton found that with a Republican in the White House, the party split in Congress after a midterm appears to matter relatively little for stock returns.
 The finding cuts across congressional combinations. The firm's measure does not tie the average to Republican control of the House, Democratic control of the Senate or any other single arrangement.
 The figure has a narrow scope. It covers only periods with a Republican president. It does not describe how stocks have performed after midterms under Democratic presidents.
 The word "around" also matters. Franklin Templeton's number is an approximate average over a period stretching back to the 1950s. It is not a precise return for any single year.
 The research applies to the current setup. President Donald Trump, a Republican, has half his term left after the 2026 midterms. That places today's market inside the scenario Franklin Templeton's average describes.
 Some House and Senate races remain uncalled. Under Franklin Templeton's measure, those outstanding results do not change which scenario applies. The average covers every chamber combination under a Republican president.
 The figure works on a 12-month horizon. It says nothing about how stocks move in the days or weeks right after an election result.
 The finding concerns returns for stocks broadly. It does not speak to how any single company, sector or commodity performs under a given lineup.
 An average blends many periods into one number. Individual 12-month stretches within that history can land above or below it. The reported figure comes without the strongest or weakest years behind it.
 A Republican president with a Democratic Congress, the most common split since the 1950s 
 Illustration: Quartz
 A Republican president paired with Democratic majorities in both the House and the Senate has been the most common arrangement since the 1950s, according to research from Franklin Templeton. The 2026 midterms appear to have produced that setup again.
 The Associated Press has Democrats holding majorities in both chambers. Some races have not yet been called. President Donald Trump has half of his term left. If the Democratic majorities hold, he will serve the rest of that term alongside a Congress controlled by the other party.
 Until the remaining races are called, the match between today's Washington and that historical pattern is provisional.
 Franklin Templeton places this balance of power inside a wider finding. Under a Republican president, the way Congress divides after a midterm appears to matter relatively little for stock returns, the firm found. That conclusion covers each combination of House and Senate control in its research.
 A Democratic hold on both chambers is one of those combinations, not an exception to the pattern. The firm's average return figure for Republican presidencies applies across every congressional split. It is not a number tied to the Democratic-Congress setup alone.
 The configuration finding and the return finding answer different questions. One describes how often this balance of power has occurred since the 1950s. The other describes how stocks have performed across all post-midterm splits under Republican presidents.
 Both findings share a time frame. Each covers the decades since the 1950s, not the full history of U.S. midterms. The return finding applies only to Republican presidencies. The research, as reported, offers no comparable conclusion for Democratic presidents.
 Frequency on its own does not point to a market direction. A setup being common means it has recurred often in the record. It does not mean stocks behave differently under it than under the other splits Franklin Templeton examined.
 SentimenTrader's November-to-April midterm pattern since the 1930s 
 Illustration: Quartz
 SentimenTrader found the stock market has not fallen from Nov. 1 of a midterm year to April of the following year at any point since the 1930s. The window is set by the calendar, not by which party wins.
 The window opens just before the vote. U.S. midterm elections are held on the Tuesday after the first Monday in November. That rule puts election day between Nov. 2 and Nov. 8. Nov. 1 always comes first.
 In 2026, election day fell on Nov. 3. The SentimenTrader window opened two days earlier.
 From there, the stretch takes in the vote count, the weeks when close races are called and the first months of the new political arrangement.
 The window also spans a change of Congress. Under the 20th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, congressional terms begin at noon on Jan. 3. Lawmakers elected in November take office that January, well before the window closes in April.
 For the current cycle, the stretch runs from Nov. 1, 2026 into April 2027. It includes the start of the 120th Congress, with Democratic majorities in both chambers serving alongside a Republican president.
 Because the window is defined by dates, the record is not tied to any single election result. Midterms since the 1930s have produced gains for each party at different times. The pattern held across those outcomes.
 The record speaks to direction, not size. Under that measure, a small rise and a large rise register the same way.
 The pattern also covers the stretch as a whole. As reported, it says nothing about how far stocks may have dipped within the window before recovering.
 The research, as reported, comes without an average gain, a range of outcomes or a breakdown by election result. It also offers no explanation for why stocks have held up over this stretch.
 Why past midterm market patterns are not a forecast 
 Illustration: Quartz
 A historical stock market pattern around midterm elections describes what has already happened, not what will happen next. Investopedia makes this point directly in its coverage of the 2026 midterms. Past patterns do not amount to a forecast.
 Investopedia published that coverage on Nov. 3, 2026, and updated it on Nov. 4. The caveat sits beside the longest-running midterm record in the piece. SentimenTrader found that the stock market has not fallen over the stretch from Nov. 1 of a midterm year to April of the next year. The firm found no such decline at any point since the 1930s.
 Every result in that record is a past outcome. It does not set a floor under prices for the months after the 2026 vote. It does not say how large any gain might be.
 The other records in the same coverage also look backward. Bespoke Investment Group's observation about the S&P 500 covers the period since the Great Financial Crisis. Franklin Templeton's return averages reach back to the 1950s. Each describes how markets behaved under earlier combinations of power in Washington.
 The 2026 cycle brings its own results. The Associated Press has Democrats holding majorities in both the House and the Senate in 2026, with some races still uncalled. President Donald Trump has half his term left. That outcome will add one more entry to the historical record. It does not mean the coming months will resemble earlier cycles.
 Investopedia's key takeaways describe the limits in two layers. The first concerns the overall market. Many experts, the article reports, believe election outcomes have a limited effect on market-level returns.
 The second layer concerns individual assets. Specific stocks, commodities and cryptocurrencies could be moved by policy changes, according to the same takeaways. A pattern built on broad market returns says nothing about how a single company, oil, gold or a cryptocurrency will respond to a policy change.
 The two layers point in different directions. A long market-wide record can hold while particular holdings move on policy news. An index-level history of midterm years cannot stand in for an outlook on any one investment.
